outline.description: Overview of the principal parties, the trademarks in dispute, the services provided, and the procedural steps that led the case to the Federal Circuit.
subtopics: Apex Bank: Tennessee‑chartered retail bank with no credit‑card service
CC Serve Corp.: credit‑card servicing company holding ASPIRE registration
ASPIRE BANK: Apex’s proposed word and design marks for banking services
Initial 2(d) opposition filed by CC Serve in February 2020
TTAB refusal based on likelihood of consumer confusion
Appeal to the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, 2025

outline.chapter_title: Legal Framework for Trademark Oppositions and Likelihood‑of‑Confusion Analysis
outline.description: Explanation of the Lanham Act provisions, the TTAB’s role, appellate review standards, and the role of the DuPont likelihood‑of‑confusion factors in opposition proceedings.
subtopics: Lanham Act §1052(d) objective: refusal of registration when confusion is likely
TTAB as the first‑level decisionmaker in trademark opposition proceedings
Appellate review: de novo review of legal conclusions, substantial evidence for findings of fact
Introduction to the DuPont factors and focus on factors two, six, and one
The interplay between legal standards and factual findings in likelihood analysis
Definition of substantial evidence per Supreme Court and appellate precedent
Relevant case law establishing the application of DuPont factors

outline.chapter_title: DuPont Factor 2: Similarity of Services and the Likelihood‑of‑Confusion Analysis
outline.description: Detailed examination of the Board’s determination that Apex’s and CC Serve’s services are substantially similar, the legal reasoning applied, and the court’s confirmation of that finding.
subtopics: Dictionary‑based definition of “credit card services” and its expansion
Comparison of “banking/financing services” to credit‑card issuance
Finding that the services are “legally identical, in part”
Use of third‑party registrations to support similarity assessment
Heavy weight attributed to factor 2 by the Board
Court’s agreement: substantial evidence backs the Board’s similarity conclusion

outline.chapter_title: DuPont Factors 6 and 1: Scope of Third‑Party Marks and Commercial Impression
outline.description: Analysis of the Board’s errors in limiting the universe of third‑party marks considered under factor six, the resulting impact on factor one's assessment of mark appearance and commercial impression, and the appellate court’s remand directive.
subtopics: Factor 6: requirement of the spectrum of similar marks on similar goods
Board’s narrow definition of the relevant public (credit‑card consumers only)
Exclusion of 42 other third‑party marks using "Aspire" in broader banking services
Interdependence of factor 6 with factor 2’s similarity finding
Factor 1: reliance on commercial impression and mark appearance
Vacating factor 1 due to altered factor 6 analysis
Remand instruction: reconsider scope of third‑party marks and reassess commercial strength

outline.description: Summary of the court’s decision, its repercussions for TTAB practice and trademark opposition strategy, and key lessons for students of intellectual‑property law.
subtopics: Final disposition: affirm factor two, vacate factors six and one, remand
Clarification that “similar goods” need only be related, not identical
Emphasis on accurately defining the universe of third‑party marks in factor six
Importance of evidence on commercial strength or weakness for scope of protection
Appellate review rules underscore the need for substantial evidence on factual findings
Implications for drafting opposition arguments and evaluating likelihood of confusion
